lesson_title: Co Is Not CO: Reading the Periodic Table Like a Street Map
hook_text: Co is a shiny metal. CO is a poisonous gas. One capital letter is the difference.
clip_script: The Periodic Table is a street map for 118 families of atoms. Every family has a symbol on its gate, capital first, small second. That rule matters: Co is cobalt, a metal. CO, two capitals, is carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas. Some gates use old Latin: Fe for iron, Na for sodium, Au for gold. The 18 streets going down are groups, and families on one street behave alike. Street 1, sodium and potassium, fizz wildly in water. Street 18, the noble gases, hardly react with anyone. The 7 roads across are periods, and they change from shiny metals on the left to non-metals on the right. A staircase line splits the town: metals left, non-metals right, semi-metals like silicon right on the line, inside every cellphone chip. And every block has an ID: the atomic number, the protons. Sodium, 11. Its mass number, 23, counts protons and neutrons together. So neutrons: 23 minus 11, that is 12.
visual_style: A cartoon town map laid over the Periodic Table; gates show symbols with Co and CO side by side; streets light up for groups and roads for periods; a staircase line glows; a sodium nucleus fills with 11 red and 12 grey balls.
pacing: A sharp hook on Co and CO, a quick map tour, a beat on the staircase, a clean counting finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count the neutrons in a chlorine atom.
